list.listitem: Consider epidural abscess and obtain imaging in patients with back pain and fever or neurologic deficit. B

Obtain ESR and CRP for patients with back pain and risk factors (diabetes mellitus; IV drug use; indwelling catheter; recent spinal surgery or instrumentation; a contiguous infection site such as psoas muscle abscess, osteomyelitis, skin infection); if abnormal, obtain imaging. B
MRI without and with contrast is the test of choice to identify epidural abscess, although direct abscess drainage and culture confirm the diagnosis and guide antibiotic treatment. B
Begin empiric antibiotic therapy with coverage of common causative organisms. B
Consult neurosurgery for consideration of surgical intervention. Selected patients can be managed medically. B

background.definition: An epidural abscess is a collection of infected material between the outer covering of the brain or spinal cord and the bones of the skull or spine.

list.listitem: 0.02 to 0.51 cases per 1000 hospital admissions per year.
Male to female ratio is approximately 2:1.

Authors of a systematic review of 22 papers reporting serious spinal pathology among 41,320 patients presenting to the Emergency Department with low back pain found a prevalence of 0% to 1.9% for infectious disorders.

Based on the Nationwide Inpatient Sample of over 3.7 million epidural procedures, there were no reported cases of epidural abscess among the 2.3 million obstetric cases and 7.2 per 100,000 (95% CI 5.8-8.7) catheterizations among non-obstetric cases.

In a Japanese study using the Diagnosis Procedure Combination database including 3,833,620 surgical patients who underwent neuraxial anesthesia, the incidence of spinal epidural abscess was 10 (7 to 13) per one million patients. There were significantly fewer complications associated with spinal anesthesia compared with epidural or combined spinal epidural anesthesia (odds ratio 0.15, 95% CI 0.1 to 0.3).
Authors of a report of 2 cases of spontaneous spinal epidural abscess occurring during pregnancy found only 8 other cases during pregnancy reported in the literature.

In a study based on three large medicolegal databases, of 135 cases with epidural abscess, 29 (21.5%) settled, 59 (43.7%) resulted in a defendant ruling, and 47 (34.8%) resulted in a plaintiff ruling. Plantiff verdicts were more common with delayed diagnosis or delayed treatment. Cases settled out of court were awarded a mean of $2,324,170 and plaintiffs received a mean award of $4,291,400.
The most commonly isolated organisms are staph species, especially Staphylococcus aureus (60%).
In a series of 101 cases from a single institution from 2004 to 2014, 25% of S. aureus isolates were methicillin-resistant. No organism was identified in 16% of cases.
Streptococcus pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Escherichia coli are other common causative organisms.
Rare causes include Brucella species, fungi, and mycobacteria including M. tuberculosis.
Parasites have also been reported as etiologic agents in the literature.

Authors of a case series of six consecutive patients with COVID-19 and primary spinal epidural abscess managed surgically over a 2-month period raised concerns about the coexistence of these two entities. They posited that this association might be related to COVID-19-related endotheliitis (inflammation of the corneal endothelium) with retrograde bacterial invasion to the correspondent spinal epidural space.

Spinal epidural abscess has been reported following use of chemoradiation for esophageal cancer, immunomodulatory treatment with biologic agents, nerve root injection, acupuncture and wet-cupping therapy, fishbone perforation, cat-scratch disease, and dental infection.

Epidural abscesses may be caused by skin infections over the spine, inoculation of the epidural space, vertebral osteomyelitis, or hematogenous spread. In one meta-analysis with a total of 915 cases, skin abscesses and furuncles were the most common source of infection.

In a case series of 101 patients at a single institution, route of infection was identified in 52% of cases with bacteremia being most common (26%), followed by recent surgery/procedure (21%) and spinal injection (6%).
No primary site is found in 50% of patients.

In a meta-analysis of 738 patients from multiple studies, epidural abscess occurred most often in the thoracic or thoracolumbar spine (42%), followed by lumbar or lumbosacral (30%) and then cervical or cervicothoracic spine (26%).
Based on a large RCT, a single, preoperative dose of cefuroxime significantly reduces the risk of organ-space infection, including epidural abscess, after surgery for herniated disc.
Consider epidural abscess and obtain imaging in patients with back pain and fever or neurologic deficit, especially for those with risk factors. C

Risk factors for epidural abscess include diabetes mellitus; IV drug use; indwelling catheter; recent spinal surgery or instrumentation; a contiguous infection site such as psoas muscle abscess, osteomyelitis, skin infection; and immunocompromise. B
Obtain ESR and CRP levels for patients with risk factors; order imaging if either is abnormal or with high clinical suspicion. B
MRI without and with contrast is the preferred imaging study. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Similar to abscess but may have history of direct open trauma; gradually progressing localized pain, increasing in severity
Less likely to have fever or elevated WBC, ESR, CRP
Key aspects include presence of neck pain, positive Kernig's sign, and Brudzinski's sign

Loss of spinal cord function over several hours to several weeks. Symptoms depend on affected segment and begin with sudden onset of back pain, muscle weakness, or abnormal sensations in the toes and feet that can rapidly progress to paralysis
History of trauma/procedure; if involving the head; look for headache, nausea, seizures, or focal deficits. Spinal hematoma mimics disc herniation
Observe for other clues such as cancer history, weight loss
Less likely to have fever, leukocytosis, or focal neurologic deficits

list.listitem: Consider spinal epidural abscess when a patient presents with back pain and neurologic deficit, fever, spinal tenderness, weakness of the extremities, bladder and/or bowel incontinence, paresthesia, or marked changes in reflexes. Fever is not always present.

A history of recent spinal manipulation including surgery, trauma, and epidural anesthesia should raise concerns for the possibility of epidural abscess formation. Other risk factors include diabetes, immunosuppression, IV drug use, and presence of an indwelling catheter. Authors of a systematic review of 22 papers found only a single study identifying risk factors for epidural abscess which included IV drug use, indwelling vascular catheter, and other infection site.

Authors of a systematic review of case reports and case series with a total of 915 patients found that 66% presented with fever, 71% with back pain, 20% with spinal irritation, and 17% with local tenderness. Neurologic deficits were present in a minority: 31% with paraparesis or paraplegia, 26% with muscle weakness, 24% with incontinence, and 13% with sensory deficits.

Ravikovitch proposed a four-phase classification of signs and symptoms: (1) midline back pain, usually at the level of the abscess; (2) radicular pain and fever; (3) sensory and motor neurologic deficits and bowel/bladder dysfunction; and (4) total paralysis. Prognosis worsens in later phases. Patients in phase 2 may have abnormal Kernig's and Lhermitte's signs, as well as Brudzinski's reflex.

The white blood cell count (WBC), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and C-reactive protein (CRP) are often elevated but are nonspecific. In a large series, the average WBC was 15,700, with a range from 1500 to 42,000. However, almost all patients have either an elevated ESR or an elevated CRP.
Obtain blood, sputum, and urine cultures, even though it is not uncommon for specimens to be negative. A gram stain and culture of abscess fluid confirms the causative organism.
CT-guided needle biopsy can be used to obtain tissue or material for culture, especially in cases of diskitis or vertebral osteomyelitis.

The American College of Radiology (revised 2021) recommends MRI without and with contrast of the affected spine segment as the initial diagnostic test of choice. Nuclear medicine studies such as skeletal scintigraphy, gallium scan, and FDG-PET/CT may be helpful in equivocal or select cases. Radiography and CT may be appropriate for assessing spinal stability and alignment, osseous integrity or the status of spine instrumentation or spine implants. .
Lumbar puncture is not necessary for diagnosis and should be avoided since it may potentially spread bacteria into the subarachnoid space.

A clinical decision rule was proposed that mandated MRI in patients with back pain and fever or neurologic deficit. For patients with risk factors for epidural abscess (IV drug use, diabetes, immunocompromise, recent spinal surgery or instrumentation, indwelling catheter, or distant site of infection), ESR and CRP were obtained. If either was abnormal, imaging was also ordered ().

Use of this protocol for 5 years (compared with the 9 years prior to its use) reduced diagnostic delay from 84% to 9%. The protocol was 97% sensitive (1 out of 31 patients was missed) and 56% specific.

In a retrospective study of MRI ordering for suspected epidural abscess in one emergency department without use of a formal decision rule, the yield was very low (7/106 [6.6%] had spinal infection, two with epidural abscess).
See for a suggested approach to diagnosis.
Initiate empiric antibiotic therapy to cover common causative organisms. B
Therapeutic options consist of surgery or medical management with antibiotics for selected patients. B
Treatment with antibiotics for epidural abscess is usually 4 to 6 weeks or longer, depending on the causative organism. C
Frequent neurologic evaluation and a repeat MRI are recommended to evaluate progress. C
Conservative management requires early identification of the causative organism, continuous availability of imaging modalities, and close follow-up.

A standard antibiotic regimen cannot be derived from published results. The choice of antibiotic is based on preferences of the clinician and institution, resistance testing, and country of treatment. Duration of antibiotic treatment is usually 4 to 6 weeks, but it may be as long as 12 weeks. Antibiotics should initially be given IV, but they may be continued orally.
Empiric antibiotic therapy should include coverage against gram-positive cocci and gram-negative bacilli with a combination of antibiotics.

Antistaphylococcal penicillins (e.g., nafcillin 100-200 mg/kg/d IV divided every 4-6 hours with max of 12 g/d) or third-generation cephalosporins (e.g., cefotaxime 1-2 g IM/IV every 8-12 hours or ceftriaxone 1-2 g IM/IV every 24 hours) provide coverage for most causative organisms and cross the blood-brain barrier. Given the increased frequency of methicillin-resistant S. aureus, the addition of vancomycin should be considered.

Failure of medical management is increased with presence of the following factors: diabetes, malignancy, documented MRSA infection, neurologic impairment, pathologic or compression fracture in affected levels, CRP >115 mg/L, WBC >12,500, ring-like enhancement on advanced imaging and posteriorly-located abscesses.

Failure of medical management in patients with risk factors occurs in up to 75% compared with 8.3% to 25% in patients without risk factors. Authors of a meta-analysis of 12 studies with 489 medically-treated patients and of a systematic review including 14 studies reported nearly identical pooled risk of failed medical management of 29.3% (95% CI 21.4%-37.2%) abd 29.4%. In the latter report, risk factors for failed medical management included acute neurological compromise, diabetes mellitus, increasing age and Staphylococcus aureus.

In a single institution case series, of 432 patients initially managed nonoperatively, factors associated with treatment failure in 99 patients (27%) were presenting motor deficit, pathologic or compression fracture in affected levels, active malignancy, diabetes mellitus, sensory changes, and dorsal location of abscess. The area under the curve for their nomogram, created using these factors, was 0.82.
Neurosurgical consultation is recommended to consider conservative medical management of epidural abscess versus surgical intervention.
Multiple procedures exist for surgical intervention including anterior decompression, percutaneous abscess drainage, and laminotomy. However, currently, laminectomy is the procedure of choice.

Minimally invasive approaches have been reported as successful based on case series, including minimally-invasive biopsy/culture/irrigation and oblique corpectomy without fusion for cervical epidural abscess.

In a single-center retrospective review of two different surgeries conducted on 31 octogenarians with ventrally located cervical spinal epidural abscess, both anterior cervical discectomy with fusion or corpectomy resulted in improved blood infection parameters and neurological status at discharge.
Early surgical intervention (<24 hours) may confer benefit for neurologic outcome.

Indications for surgical intervention include increased osseous involvement, increased paraspinal abscess formation, neurologic deficit, failure to respond to conservative therapy, deformity with or without incapacitating spinal pain, or failure to obtain necessary culture material.

Historically, mortality ranged from 25% to 40% for epidural abscess prior to combined neurosurgical intervention and antibiotic therapy; it now ranges from 7% to 15%. B
Mortality rates remain higher for patients with serious underlying conditions.

In a single institution review of 1053 patients with epidural abscess, the 8 independent risk factors predictive of 90-day mortality, which occurred in 134 (12.7%), were active malignancy, age >65 years, hemodialysis, diabetes mellitus, endocarditis, pre-treatment motor deficit, white blood cell count >15 x 109 cells/L, and symptom duration for 24-72 hours.

Neurologic deficits are common in spinal epidural abscess but may be minimized with early diagnosis, although permanent neurologic sequelae remain common after infection. B
In one case series of 36 patients, 22 fully recovered. In another case series of 23 patients with late diagnosis spinal epidural abscess accompanied by impaired neurologic status in 21 of whom 11 had paraplegia, laminectomy and evacuation of abscess resulted in good functional outcome in almost half.
In a series of patients undergoing inpatient rehabilitation following spinal epidural abscess, there was significant recovery from neurologic deficits. B

Neurologic evaluation and a repeat MRI are recommended after resolution of symptoms to monitor resolution of infection. However, recent data suggest that findings on follow-up MRI may not be helpful for patients improving clinically following therapy. B

A 90-day unplanned reoperation rate of 19.9% was found using an institutional cohort of 642 patients from 5 medical centers who underwent surgery for a spinal epidural abscess. Using the US National Surgical Quality Improvement Program (NSQIP) database including 951 patients, these authors found a 30-day unplanned reoperation rate of 12.3%. Risk factors for 30-day reoperation in the institutional cohort were preoperative urinary incontinence, ventral location of abscess relative to thecal sac, cervical abscess, preoperative wound infection, and leukocytosis (Area under the curve=0.65). Only cervical spine abscess was an identified risk factor for the NSQIP database cohort.

cell.label: Patient with back pain: fever or neurologic deficit?
Risk factors for epidural abscess (diabetes mellitus, IV drug user, immunosuppression, indwelling catheter, recent spine surgery, distant site of infection)?
Order imaging (MRI; if contraindicated or unavailable, then CT with myelogram).
Blood, urine, sputum cultures. Order empiric IV antibiotics and obtain neurosurgery and infectious disease consults to consider surgical versus medical management.
